text: GRAPHICALABSTRACT
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > GRAPHICALABSTRACT

text: The major mechanism of corrosion inhibition effect by nicotinic acid (NA) is to form a passivation film which adsorbs on cobalt (Co) surface so as to strengthen the surface impedance and isolate the corrosion medium. In an alkaline environment (pH 10), NA exists in the form of Nic 2− ions, which are negatively charged. Driven by electrostatic forces and Van der Waals forces between NA molecule (N atom and the carboxyl) and cobalt atom, Nic 2− ions are appealed to the Co(OH) 2, leading to the appearance of Co(II)-NA molecule groups. NA molecules produce a single or multilayer self-assembled Co(II)-NA film on the cobalt surface and further preven the corrosion on Co film.

text: ABSTRACT
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > ABSTRACT

text: Cobalt (Co) is the interconnect metal of integrated circuits with the feature size of 10 nm and below, and Co corrosion is the main problem in cobalt interconnect chemical mechanical polishing (CMP). The introduction of inhibitors is one of the most ideal approaches to reduce corrosion. In this work, useful insights into the corrosion inhibition performance of nicotinic acid (NA), a green inhibitor, on cobalt film in alkaline medium were investigated via electrochemical characterization, surface analysis, quantum chemical calculation, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulation, as well as the adsorption mechanism at atomic level was explored. NA belongs to anodic erosion inhibitor and its inhibition efficiency reached a maximum of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM pH 10, which was identified by the contact angle and potentiodynamic polarization (PDP) test. The elec trochemical impedance spectra (EIS) suggested that the surface resistance was enhanced to prevent corrosion. Free energy obtained from the Langmuir model indicates that NA molecules are physically and spontaneously adsorbed on cobalt surface.
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > ABSTRACT

text: XPS results further confirmed this point, which reveals that NA exists in the form of Nic 2− in alkaline solution and forms a Co(OH)_2(Nic^2-) molecule group (Co(II)-NA) on Co surface. Additionally, quantum chemical calculations based on density function theory (DFT) have approved that C–N bond and carboxyl group are the active sites of NA molecule and form the most significant electrostatic adsorption force with cobalt atoms. Moreover, it can be inferred from MD simulations that NA molecules are spontaneously and physically adsorbed on the cobalt surface at a certain angle. In a word, NA manifests its effectiveness in corrosion inhibition of cobalt and will become a potential cobalt CMP inhibitor. The research methods and results of this paper are beneficial to the study of the adsorption characteristics and inhibition mechanism of inhibitors on the metal surface, and provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry.

text: 1. Introduction
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: As the feature size of integrated circuits (ICs) shrinks below 10 nm, cobalt is the most promising material to replace tungsten (W) and copper (Cu) as the front and intermediate lines owing to its great resistance to electromigration and good performance in step coverage [1]. In addition, the barrier layer of cobalt interconnect ICs is thinner than that of copper [2,3]. After cobalt film deposition, the wafer surface is uneven, so chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) is used in IC manufacturing process to realize local and global planarization through the coordina tion of chemical action and mechanical action [4].
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: However, Co is prone to being corroded by CMP slurry, which con tains many aggressive chemicals, e.g., oxidizers and complexing agents, in which H_2O_2 is widely used to increase removal rate of cobalt as a green oxidizer [5,6]. Yang et al. [7] studied the corrosion of Co in alkaline medium containing H_2O_2 and found that lots of pits were appeared in the presence of 0.1 wt% H_2O_2,, and at some locations, the coating layer was fragmented and peeling occurred. In order to reduce the corrosion of Co surface, many methods and new chemicals have been introduced into the study of cobalt. Badawy et al. [8] investigated the corrosion of Co in alkaline solution and suggested that the potential of Co can be increased by increasing the pH value of the solution to slow down the corrosion rate. Accordingly, all experiments in this study were carried out under alkaline conditions.
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: In recent years, the addition of corrosion inhibitors has been proved to be an effective measure to inhibit corrosion of metal materials [9 11]. Many studies show that organic inhibitor molecules containing elements such as C, N, and O are often more effective in corrosion prevention, among which benzotriazole (BTA) is a common inhibitor and has been broadly commercialized [12 14]. The corrosion inhibition effect of BTA was firstly reported by Cotton et al. [15], and since then researchers have carried out a lot of researches on BTA [ 9, 1 6, 1 7 ]. However, some current studies reported that BTA has a poor inhibition effect on Co corrosion in corrosive medium. Yang et al. [7] characterized the surface morphology of Co in the solution containing BTA and H_2O_2 by SEM, and concluded that BTA could not effectively reduce the pitting caused by H_2O_2 on Co surface. Similarly, Lei et al. [18] suggested that BTA is no longer applicable to Co CMP by means of surface morphology test. In addition, the toxicity of BTA also limits its application in CMP [19,20].
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: Therefore, scholars have been committed to developing green and effective corrosion inhibitors for Co CMP, such as organic acid and vi tamins [21–23].
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: Notably, nicotinic acid, which belongs to the B3 group of vitamins, is widely used as an intermediate in the synthesis of various pharmaceuticals and shows favorable potential in corrosion inhibition effect. Mohamed et al. [23] investigated the polishing behavior and defects of cobalt samples with an aqueous mixture of H_2O_2, oxalic acid (OA), and nicotinic acid at pH 10. The results show that the alkaline solution including 80 mM NA can broadly reduce the corrosion current of cobalt samples and galvanic erosion between cobalt and copper, proving that NA can operate as an inhibitor for Co film in H_2O_2 solution. He et al. [24] concluded that NA offers a composite layer on the cobalt surface, and prevents further Co corrosion, while a combination of 10 mM NA and 5 mM TAZ minimized Co-Cu corrosion as measured by zero resistance galvanometer. Although it is confirmed that NA possesses an inhibition effect on cobalt, further studies on NA, such as the interaction process between NA and Co, the adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface and so on, have not been reported.
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: Studying the adsorption of corrosion inhibitor on the metal surface is of great significance to explore the corrosion inhibition mechanism. This work mainly studies the inhibitory effect of NA on cobalt corrosion in alkaline medium, as well as the formation and mechanism of [NA-Co] complex.
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: Studies on the performance of inhibitor molecules only by conventional chemical experiments and characteristic methods are inadequate. The rapid development of theoretical chemistry provides a more scientific explanation for its research. Molecular simulation is a crucial approach to study the molecular chemical activity of corrosion inhibitors from a microscopic perspective [25,27–29]. The adsorption mechanism between inhibitors and metal substrates can be intuitively characterized by molecular simulation technology. Ma et al. [26] probed the effect of potassium oleate (PO) as a viable corrosion inhibitor for Cu films in EDTA–H_2O_2 based solution through combining chemical experiment analysis with molecular simulation. Density functional theory and molecular dynamics approaches were applied to study the inhibition mechanism at the atom level of PO on Cu(111) substrate. Yin et al. [16] evaluated the corrosion inhibition of BTA and TAZ at the molecular level via comparing quantum chemical descriptors. Therefore, it is necessary to further study the quantum chemical properties of NA and micro adsorption mechanism of NA on Co surface.
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 1. Introduction

text: Considering that NA is an inexpensive, green, and easily available organic inhibitor, it was introduced into the alkaline (pH 10) solution. The molecular structure of NA is shown in Fig. 1. Contact angle and PDP measurements were carried out to determine the optimal concentration of NA. The passive film of NA was investigated by EIS, and the reaction between Co and NA was explored by XPS. Density functional theory was employed to study the properties of NA molecule. Several chemical descriptors were calculated to reveal active sites of NA molecule and the electron transfer characteristics between NA and Co atoms, as well as MD simulation was conducted to study the adsorption configuration, adsorption stability and adsorption sites of NA on Co surface. This work provides a more in-depth insight into the development of alkaline cobalt CMP slurry.

text: 2.1. Materials
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 2.1. Materials

text: Cobalt coupons (2 cm * 2 cm) cut from a 12-inch. cobalt blanket wafer were used to accomplish the contact angle test and electrochemical experiments. Before each experiment, the coupons were immersed in 0.025 M citric acid (C_6H_8O_7,, CA, 99 %) solution for 5 min to remove the oxide layer on the film surface, then rinsed with deionized water (DIW) and dried with nitrogen ( N _ 2). After CA treatment, the cobalt specimens were immersed in NA ( C _ 6 H _ 5 NO _ 2, 99.5 %) solutions with different concentrations (40, 50, 60, 70, 80 mM) for 5 min. The pH of each inhibitor solution was adjusted to 10.00 with KOH and H_3PO_4. Eventually, these cobalt coupons were rinsed with DIW and dried with Ν _ 2 to obtain different samples.

text: The surface chemical compounds of cobalt samples were explored by X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS, ESCALA250Xi, Thermo, USA), which was stimulated by an Al-Kα anode and operated at a base pressure of 5 × 1 0 ^- 1 0 mbar and a constant power of 150 W. text: 2.3. Electrochemical experiments
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 2.3. Electrochemical experiments

text: All PDP measurements were performed on a CHI660E workstation with a three-electrode system (Chenhua, Shanghai). The treated cobalt coupon was wrapped with waterproof tape with an exposed area of 0.3 8 cm ^2, which was used as the working electrode, and saturated mercury electrode (SCE) and platinum (Pt) electrode (the size was 2 cm * 2 cm) as the reference electrode and the counter electrode, respectively. Different concentrations of NA liquids (pH 10) were taken as electrolyte solutions. The open circuit potential (OCP) was tested incessantly for 600 s to acquire more stable results. The Tafel plots of the Co electrode were gained by PDP curve test at the scanning rate of 5 mV/s within the voltage range of OCP ± 0.3 : V The EIS measurements were conducted on cobalt electrode via potentiostat (ZSRS-UI5022), OCP as initial value and 10 mV peak-topeak sine waves with the frequency in the range of 0.1 Hz to 10 kHz as AC perturbation signals. The EIS data were fitted and rectified by the complex nonlinear least squares (CNLS) method in Zsimpwin software.

text: The Forcite module was employed to operate MD simulations. The ideal Co(111) surface was selected as the adsorption object owing to its high atomic density and low Miller index. The inhibitor molecule and Co (111) crystal system with the size of 6 × 6 × 8 and containing a 40 Å vacuum layer were optimized before the start of each dynamics simulation. In order to obtain stable adsorption configuration of the inhibitor on the Co(111) surface, MD simulation was carried out at the ‘Universal force field and QEq ^* charge. The total energy was calculated by the summation method of the atom-based electrostatic and van der Waals. All MD simulations were based on NVT thermodynamics with an absolute temperature of 298 K, a time step of 1 fs, and a total simulation time of 1000 ps.

text: 3.1. Contact angle test analysis
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 3.1. Contact angle test analysis

text: The adsorption of organic molecules on the metal surface will change its hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity and alters the contact angle of metal surface, while fresh metal surfaces usually present hydrophilicity, hence the contact angle reflects the adsorption effect of the inhibitor [30]. Fig. 2 illustrates contact angle of cobalt samples treated with different concentrations of NA and compared with that treated with CA. After CA treatment, the natural oxide layer on the cobalt surface was removed, and the contact angle of the cobalt surface reduced from 5 5 ^° to 47◦, obtaining the fresh cobalt surface [31]. The contact angle increased to 6 7 ^° following 40 mM NA treatment and increased steadily with the increase of NA concentration until the maximum contact angle reached 8 3 ^° when the concentration was 80 mM. When the concentrations of NA were 90 and 100 mM, the contact angles were 82◦ and 83◦, respectively, which remained basically unchanged compared with that of 80 mM. These results show that when the concentration of NA is greater than 80 mM, the adsorption of NA molecules on the cobalt surface reaches saturation.

text: 3.2. Electrochemical test analysis
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 3.2. Electrochemical test analysis

text: According to the contact angle results, PDP tests were carried out to evaluate the effect of corrosion inhibition of NA with the concentration less than 100 mM on cobalt electrode. Fig. 3 shows the PDP curves of cobalt electrode treated with different NA concentrations.
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 3.2. Electrochemical test analysis

text: With the introduction of NA, both the anode and cathode branches of Tafel curves have the tendency to extend to the region of low corrosion current density. Compared with the cathode branches, the corrosion current density of the anode branches differs from one another markedly, i.e. the reduction reaction rate of dissolved oxygen at the cathode basically remains unchanged, while the metal ionization process occurring at the anode is inhibited. Accordingly, nicotinic acid belongs to the anodic corrosion inhibitor. The linear region of anodic branch, named as passivation region, proves that NA molecules gradually adhere to the cobalt surface to form a protective film and reduce the corrosion degree. It is noteworthy that the slope at the end of the 40 mM NA anode branch (circled in red) sinks, which is caused by the incompactness of the passivation film as the local corrosion medium may interact with the metal through the protective layer to aggravate the metal ionization. The illustration in Fig. 3 shows the PDP test curves of cobalt electrode in NA solutions with concentrations of 80, 90 and 100 mM, respectively.

text: 3.3. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy analysis
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 3.3. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy analysis

text: EIS measurement was used to analyze the passivation effect of physically adsorbed protective film on cobalt surface in alkaline medium. Fig. 5(a) shows the Nyquist impedance spectra of the Co electrodes in different concentrations of NA, which can better understand the structure of passivation layer. Since the Nyquist curve is a 1/4 arc, the charge transfer controls the erosion on cobalt/alkaline medium interface, and the equivalent circuit is a simple model formed by electron exchange on passivation film. In the event that the general shape of the impedance spectra does not change with the introduction of inhibitors, the reaction principle of the corrosive medium could be considered as unaffected [35]. Meanwhile the radius of the spectrum increases with the increase of NA concentration, suggesting that the adsorption film turns to be more completed [36]. The radius of imped ance spectrum reaches the maximum when the concentration of NA is 80 mM, which is consistent with PDP results.

section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 3.4. XPS analysis

text: XPS was introduced to confirm the chemical composition of cobalt samples to further analyze the reaction state of cobalt surface. The XPS spectra and corresponding Co 2p spectra of cobalt samples after being treated with CA and immersed in 80 mM NA are shown in Fig. 6. Fig. 6 (a) shows that the two curves have three distinct peaks (C, O, and Co). In contrast, the peak intensities of C, O, and Co soaked in NA are signifi cantly higher than that of soaked in citric acid. This phenomenon is consistent with the element of NA molecules, and it can be inferred that inhibitor NA and its relative products can successfully assemble on the cobalt surface, issuing in the change of peak intensity of homologous elements. In addition, the appearance of N peak on the Co sample’s surface is induced by the pyrazole ring in the NA molecule [32].

text: 3.5. DFT calculation analysis
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 3.5. DFT calculation analysis

text: Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) theory has been widely applied in the field of chemical structure to evaluate the efficiency of inhibitors, as well as explore the mechanism of interaction between inhibitors and metal surfaces [42–44]. Hence, a series of quantum chemical parameters, such as the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) energy levels, and the energy gap (ΔE) were calculated by DFT method. Firstly, the structure of NA molecular was optimized, and then properties of the frontier orbital of NA molecule were evaluated.

text: HOMO has the electron donor nature with loose binding to its elec trons, while LUMO possesses the ability to accept electrons, which is usually called electron acceptor, with a strong affinity for electrons.

text: Generally, the higher HOMO energy or a lower LUMO energy manifests a mightier capability of molecular electron pairs to transfer or vacant orbitals to accept electron pairs. For corrosion inhibitors, this also means a more violent trend of binding and adsorption with metal surface atoms, that is, more efficient corrosion inhibition competence [45]. On top of that, the molecule activity is strengthened with the decrease of ΔE ( Δ E = Δ E _LUMO - Δ E _HOMO), i.e. the reduction of ΔE promotes the impact of corrosion inhibition.

text: Fig. 8(a) and (b) demonstrate the optimized NA molecule and the electron cloud distribution of HOMO and LUMO. In the HOMO diagram, the electron cloud is mainly distributed on the N = C bond, while the N––C bond and the carboxyl group (-COOH) occupy the primary electron cloud of LUMO, indicating that chemical reactivity exists in the N = C bond and the -COOH. The truth that the value of ΔE for BTA ( Δ E _ BTA = 3.7 9 7 \ eV) [8] is larger than that of NA ( Δ E _ N A = 2.1 1 4 \ eV) signifies that the corrosion inhibition performance of NA surpasses that of BTA. Electrostatic potential (ESP) results can further confirm this conclusion, as shown in Fig. 8(c). The region of electrophilic with the highest negative potential is marked in red, while the blue region indicates nucleophilic. As shown in Fig. 8(d), the highest red region is located on N6 and O8, as well as the blue region covers the H14 atom, which fully suggests that the functional sites of NA on the cobalt surface are N––C bond and the carboxyl group.

Chemicals with ω greater than 1.5 eV can be classified as powerful electrophiles [49]. As ω = 1 0.9 8 1 eV for NA, the NA molecule is a relatively stable electrophilic molecule with a strong inclination to accumulate electrons from electron-rich cobalt surface [50]. text: 4. Conclusion
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 4. Conclusion

text: In this work, we focused on nicotinic acid as a potential corrosion inhibitor for cobalt CMP in alkaline medium, and the adsorption behavior of NA was systematically revealed by several characteristic techniques and molecular simulations. The results of contact angel and electrochemical test show that corrosion efficiency reached the maximum value of 86.65 % at the concentration of 80 mM. The adsorption of NA on cobalt surface follows the Langmuir adsorption isotherm, which is a spontaneous physical process. EIS further suggests that with the increase of NA concentration, the passivation film covered on cobalt surface became more complete, resulting in the increase of surface resistance. According to the results of XPS, NA molecules exist in the form of Nic ^2 - ions in alkaline environment, and physically assemble on Co(OH)_2 to form Co(II)-NA molecular groups to isolate the permeation of corrosive medium. DFT calculation and MD simulation indicate that NA molecule is adsorbed on the Co(111) surface at a certain angle through Coulomb force and van der Waals force, which are derived from the interaction of N = C bond and carboxyl in NA molecule and surface cobalt atoms.
section: Nicotinic acid as a novel inhibitor for alkaline cobalt CMP: Experiment and molecular simulation > 4. Conclusion

text: The results of this work on passive film of NA on Co surface and its microscopic properties provide a theoretical basis for optimizing the composition of Co CMP slurry, and also provide support for subsequent researches of exploring synergistic effect of NA and other slurry components. In conclusion, NA is suggested to be an effective potential inhibitor for Co CMP in IC manufacturing process. Its physical adsorption on cobalt surface will help to improve the inhibitor removal effect in post CMP cleaning.
